note: US environmental-release authorisations harvested from the APHIS BRS public data files (public domain), plus hand-curated records from other registers. Only records with a release component are included — import and interstate movement are not releases. Every position is a state centroid: APHIS publishes release states, never coordinates, so every record is precise:false and draws as a dashed ring. Canadian records come from the CFIA PNT dataset and sit at the national centroid, because that register records a national approval rather than a planting location. Everywhere else is not yet harvested.

projects.name: DIR 201 — GM wheat & barley field trial (yield enhancement)
projects.type: GM wheat and barley field trial
projects.size: 1 site, max 2 ha/yr
projects.desc: Field trial of wheat and barley genetically modified for yield enhancement. One site in Light Regional Council, South Australia, maximum two hectares per year, May 2024 to January 2029. Not permitted in human food or animal feed. Location shown at council level — open the licence page for the site conditions.

projects.name: DIR 186 — GM wheat & barley field trial (yield + abiotic stress)
projects.type: GM wheat and barley field trial
projects.size: 1 site, max 2 ha/yr
projects.desc: Field trial of wheat and barley genetically modified for yield enhancement and improved abiotic stress tolerance. One site in Light Regional Council, South Australia, maximum two hectares per year, April 2022 to January 2027. Licence conditions require isolation from other wheat and barley, secure transport and storage, and end-of-trial destruction verified by site inspection.

projects.name: DIR 204 — HB4 wheat field trial (environmental stress tolerance)
projects.size: up to 10 sites/yr, 20 ha/yr total
projects.desc: HB4 wheat, OECD unique identifier IND-ØØ412-7. Carries the HaHB4 gene from sunflower for environmental stress tolerance plus the bar gene as a glufosinate-tolerance selectable marker, introduced by biolistic transformation. Up to ten sites per year across wheat-growing areas of New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia, twenty hectares total per year, August 2024 to December 2029. Already approved for commercial cultivation in Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. Marker sits at a wheat-belt centroid because the trial is multi-state.

projects.name: DIR 165 — GM wheat field trial (iron uptake & bioavailability)
projects.size: controlled field sites
projects.desc: Wheat genetically modified for altered iron uptake, transport and bioavailability and for enhanced yield, carrying antibiotic and herbicide selectable markers. Sites and dates are not restated on the summary page used to build this record — open the licence for them. Marker parked at the national centroid, so treat the position as unknown rather than approximate.

projects.name: DIR 220 — GM multivalent cat vaccine, commercial supply
projects.size: national commercial supply
projects.desc: Commercial supply of multivalent cat vaccines containing a genetically modified component, for prevention of feline leukaemia virus infection. A commercial-supply licence is national in scope, so there is no site to place — the marker sits at the country centroid. A separate Intervet application for a GM multivalent chicken vaccine was pending at the time this record was written.

projects.name: Institute for Human Reproduction (IHR)
projects.desc: A fertility clinic reporting to the CDC's National ART Surveillance System. Medical director: David P. Cohen, MD. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. Reporting is required of every US clinic performing assisted reproduction, under the Fertility Clinic Success Rate and Certification Act, so this is close to a complete register rather than a list of members. What it records is cycles started, which is not the same as children born.

A research registration is issued to an organisation rather than to a building, so for a university it is usually the research administration office and the animals are elsewhere on campus or in another city. Rats, mice and birds bred for research are excluded from the Act's definition of an animal — the overwhelming majority of animals used, and the great majority of the genetically altered ones. What is covered here is dogs, cats, primates, rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters and farm animals. The rest is counted nowhere.

Rats, mice and birds bred for research are excluded from the Act's definition of an animal — the overwhelming majority of animals used, and the great majority of the genetically altered ones. What is covered here is dogs, cats, primates, rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters and farm animals. The rest is counted nowhere.

A research registration is issued to an organisation rather than to a building, so for a university it is usually the research administration office and the animals are elsewhere on campus or in another city. Rats, mice and birds bred for research are excluded from the Act's definition of an animal — the overwhelming majority of animals used, and the great majority of the genetically altered ones. What is covered here is dogs, cats, primates, rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters and farm animals. The rest is counted nowhere.

A research registration is issued to an organisation rather than to a building, so for a university it is usually the research administration office and the animals are elsewhere on campus or in another city. Rats, mice and birds bred for research are excluded from the Act's definition of an animal — the overwhelming majority of animals used, and the great majority of the genetically altered ones. What is covered here is dogs, cats, primates, rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters and farm animals. The rest is counted nowhere.

projects.name: 北京大学第三医院
projects.state: 北京市（18家） — 北京市海淀区花园北路49号
projects.size: 5 approved techniques
projects.desc: A medical institution approved by China's National Health Commission to perform assisted reproduction. Approved for: ICSI — a single sperm injected into the egg; IVF with embryo transfer; embryo screening before transfer; insemination with donor sperm; insemination with the partner's sperm. All of its approvals are in formal operation. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. Approval is compulsory in China and performing assisted reproduction without it is unlawful, so this list is a register rather than a directory of members. It names every approved institution in the country, which is more than almost any other state publishes. The address did not geocode, so this point sits at the centre of the province rather than at the institution.

projects.name: United Kingdom — HFEA licensed clinic register
projects.desc: The UK regulator licenses every clinic and publishes its inspection history and its ratings of the optional add-on treatments clinics sell. Most add-ons are rated red or amber - no good evidence they work - and they continue to be sold.

projects.name: United States — CDC ART clinic reporting
projects.desc: US clinics performing IVF must report cycles and outcomes. Success rates depend heavily on which patients a clinic accepts, so a clinic can raise its published figures by declining harder cases, and the data cannot show you that.

projects.name: Australia — ANZARD accredited units
projects.desc: Australia and New Zealand report through a shared database, with accreditation required to operate.

projects.name: India — no public clinic register
projects.desc: India regulates assisted reproduction under a 2021 Act and prohibited commercial surrogacy, but publishes no register of licensed clinics. Estimates of the number operating run into the thousands.

projects.name: China — no public clinic register
projects.desc: Clinics are licensed centrally by the National Health Commission and the list is not published in a form that can be read from outside.

projects.name: Russia — no public clinic register
projects.desc: A large fertility sector including commercial surrogacy for foreign patients, with no public clinic register.

projects.name: Ukraine — no public clinic register
projects.desc: A principal destination for cross-border surrogacy before 2022, with no published register of the clinics arranging it.

projects.name: Nigeria — no public clinic register
projects.desc: The largest fertility market in West Africa, with no national licensing register.

projects.name: Brazil — no public clinic register
projects.desc: Clinics report to a national system run by the medical regulator, but clinic-level data is not published.

projects.name: Mexico — no public clinic register
projects.desc: A significant destination for cross-border treatment, regulated at state level with no national register.

projects.name: Japan — no public clinic register
projects.desc: One of the highest per-capita IVF rates in the world, with clinics registered through a professional society rather than a public regulator.

projects.name: United States — USDA APHIS — licensed research facilities
projects.desc: Every registered US research facility is named, inspected, and reports annually how many dogs, cats, primates and other covered animals it used and in what pain category. The inspection reports are published per facility, specific, and almost never read. Mice, rats and birds bred for research are excluded from the governing Act, so the most detailed facility register in the world omits the overwhelming majority of the animals used in it.

projects.name: United Kingdom — Home Office — licensed establishments and annual procedures
projects.desc: Every UK establishment licensed to use animals in research is named in a public list, alongside annual procedure counts by species, severity and purpose. It is the only place in the world where both the places and the numbers are public and complete, and it exists because Parliament legislated for it in 1986 rather than because anyone offered it.

projects.name: European Union — ALURES — EU animal use database
projects.desc: Member states report animal use by species, purpose and severity, and the Commission publishes the aggregate. It counts procedures rather than places: no member state is required to name its facilities, so the European picture is a set of national totals with nothing behind them.

projects.name: Canada — CCAC — Canadian Council on Animal Care
projects.desc: Canada's system is voluntary certification by a council rather than statutory licensing. Institutions that hold federal funding must participate, aggregate numbers are published, and the certified institutions are listed — which puts Canada between the UK and the countries that publish nothing.

projects.name: China — no public facility register
projects.desc: A research system now comparable in scale to the American one. China publishes no national count of animals used and no facility register, so the size of the practice is inferred from the breeding suppliers rather than reported.

projects.name: Japan — no public facility register
projects.desc: Self-regulated through institutional committees and a professional society. No national count is published, so Japanese laboratory animal use is estimated from what the suppliers sell.

projects.name: India — no public facility register
projects.desc: Experiments are overseen by a national committee that has banned animal use for cosmetics testing and some teaching, but facility-level records are not public.

projects.name: South Korea — no public facility register
projects.desc: A large and fast-growing research sector. Aggregate figures are published annually; the institutions behind them are not named.

projects.name: Brazil — no public facility register
projects.desc: Institutions register with a national council and aggregate figures exist, but facility-level inspection records are not published.

projects.name: Russia — no public facility register
projects.desc: No public register of animal research facilities and no national count.
